description: Pharmaceutical Manufacturing Glossary - Comprehensive terms for tablet and capsule manufacturing.

terms.definition: The biologically active component in a pharmaceutical product that produces the intended therapeutic effect.
An inactive substance used as a carrier, diluent, or vehicle for the active pharmaceutical ingredient in a dosage form.
A process of agglomerating powder particles to form granules, improving flow properties and compressibility for tablet manufacturing.
A granulation process where a liquid binder solution is added to powder mixture to form granules through high-shear mixing or fluid bed processing.
A granulation process where powders are compacted using slugging or roller compaction without the addition of liquid binders.
A tablet manufacturing method where blended powders are compressed directly into tablets without prior granulation steps.
The process of mixing powders to achieve uniform distribution of API and excipients before further processing or compression.
The addition of lubricants to reduce friction during tablet ejection and prevent die-wall adhesion during compression.
The process of compacting granulated or blended powder into tablets using a tablet press under controlled force and speed.
The process of filling empty gelatin or HPMC capsules with pharmaceutical powders, granules, or liquid formulations.
Application of a thin polymer-based coating to tablets to improve appearance, taste masking, moisture protection, or controlled release.
A multi-step coating process applying successive layers of sugar-based solution to tablets for taste masking and aesthetic improvement.
The process of enclosing finished pharmaceutical products in containers for distribution, storage, and patient use.
A unit-dose packaging method where individual tablets or capsules are sealed in pre-formed cavities backed by foil or film.
A packaging method where tablets or capsules are sealed between two layers of heat-sealable material.
Packaging of finished products in large containers such as drums or cartons for bulk distribution.
The process of weighing, measuring, and issuing raw materials according to the master formula for a specific batch.
Accurate measurement of raw materials using calibrated balances according to the master formula requirements.
The process of passing powders through a sieve to remove agglomerates and ensure uniform particle size distribution.
Size reduction of particles using mechanical force to achieve desired particle size distribution for processing.
Reduction of particle size to micrometer range, typically for poorly soluble APIs to improve dissolution rate.
The process of producing uniform particle distribution in emulsions, suspensions, or semi-solid formulations.
The process of creating a stable mixture of two immiscible liquids (oil and water) using emulsifiers and mechanical energy.
The process of eliminating or destroying all forms of microbial life from equipment, containers, or products.
Heat treatment process applied to liquids to reduce microbial load without complete sterilization.
Manufacturing of sterile products in a controlled environment where pre-sterilized components are assembled under aseptic conditions.
Monitoring of airborne particles, microbial contamination, temperature, humidity, and pressure differentials in clean rooms.
A filter capable of removing at least 99.97% of particles with size 0.3 micrometers, used in clean room air handling systems.
A unidirectional airflow system that provides a particle-free environment for aseptic operations.
A controlled environment with defined limits on airborne particle concentration, temperature, and humidity for pharmaceutical manufacturing.
International standard (ISO 14644) defining air cleanliness classes based on particle concentration limits per cubic meter.
Regulations ensuring pharmaceutical products are consistently produced and controlled according to quality standards.
Quality system of management controls for research laboratories to ensure the integrity of non-clinical safety data.
Quality system ensuring pharmaceutical products are consistently stored, transported, and handled under proper conditions.
International harmonization guidelines for pharmaceutical development, quality, safety, and efficacy established by the International Council for Harmonisation.
US FDA regulation defining requirements for electronic records, electronic signatures, and audit trails in pharmaceutical operations.
US FDA cGMP regulations for pharmaceutical manufacturing, covering general provisions and finished pharmaceuticals.
European Commission guideline for computerized systems in GMP-regulated environments.
European Commission guideline for qualification and validation of equipment, utilities, and systems.
Good Manufacturing Practice guidelines published by the World Health Organization for pharmaceutical manufacturing.
UK Medicines and Healthcare products Regulatory Agency guidelines covering GMP, GLP, GCP, and GDP.
Good Automated Manufacturing Practice framework for validation of computerized systems in regulated environments.
Three-phase validation approach: IQ verifies equipment installation, OQ tests operational parameters, PQ confirms performance under actual conditions.
Documented evidence that a process, system, or method consistently produces a result meeting predetermined specifications.
Establishing by scientific evidence that a manufacturing process consistently produces a product meeting its predetermined quality attributes.
Documented evidence that cleaning procedures consistently remove residues from manufacturing equipment to predetermined limits.
Establishing that an analytical procedure is suitable for its intended purpose by demonstrating specificity, accuracy, precision, and other performance characteristics.
Systematic testing of pharmaceutical products under defined conditions to determine shelf life and storage requirements.
Stability testing at elevated conditions (40°C/75% RH for 6 months) to predict shelf life under normal storage conditions.
Stability testing under recommended storage conditions (25°C/60% RH for Zone II) for the product's shelf life period.
Forced degradation studies conducted under extreme conditions to identify potential degradation products and establish stability-indicating methods.
In vitro test measuring the rate and extent of drug release from a dosage form in simulated physiological conditions.
Test determining whether tablets or capsules break down into particles within a specified time in simulated gastrointestinal fluid.
Measurement of the force required to break a tablet, indicating its mechanical strength and friability resistance.
Test measuring the weight loss of tablets subjected to mechanical stress during tumbling, indicating resistance to chipping and abrasion.
Test measuring the uniformity of tablet weight within a batch to ensure consistent dosage delivery.
Test ensuring that individual dosage units contain the labeled amount of API within specified limits.
Analytical determination of the amount of active ingredient in a pharmaceutical product, typically expressed as percentage of label claim.
Impurities chemically related to the API, including degradation products and synthesis by-products, monitored to ensure product safety.
Organic solvents retained in drug substances or products after manufacturing, classified by ICH Q3C based on toxicity.
Measurement of moisture present in pharmaceutical products, typically determined by Karl Fischer titration.
Analytical method for precise determination of water content in pharmaceutical products using iodine-based chemistry.
Checks and tests performed during manufacturing to monitor and control process parameters and product quality.
A process variable whose variation has a direct impact on a critical quality attribute and must be monitored and controlled.
A physical, chemical, biological, or microbiological property or characteristic that must be within an appropriate limit to ensure product quality.
Systematic risk assessment tool to identify potential failure modes, their causes, and effects on process or product quality.
Cause-and-effect diagram (also called Ishikawa diagram) used to systematically identify potential root causes of a problem.
A cause-and-effect diagram developed by Kaoru Ishikawa for identifying potential factors causing an overall effect.
A bar graph arranging causes from most to least frequent, used to identify the vital few problems requiring attention.
A statistical tool with upper and lower control limits used to determine if a manufacturing process is in a state of control.
Use of statistical methods to monitor and control a manufacturing process to ensure it operates at its full potential.
Statistical measure of the inherent process variability compared to specification limits, expressed as Cp and Cpk indices.
Ratio of specification width to process width, measuring how well a process can meet specification limits assuming it is centered.
Measure of process capability accounting for process centering relative to specification limits.
Average time between equipment failures, used to measure equipment reliability and plan preventive maintenance.
Average time required to repair equipment after a failure, measuring maintenance efficiency and downtime impact.
Productivity metric calculated as Availability × Performance × Quality, measuring equipment utilization efficiency.
Systematic approach to equipment maintenance involving all employees to maximize equipment effectiveness and eliminate breakdowns.
Production methodology focused on minimizing waste while maximizing productivity and value creation.
Data-driven methodology for eliminating defects and reducing process variation to achieve 3.4 defects per million opportunities.
Six Sigma improvement cycle methodology for optimizing and stabilizing business processes.
Continuous improvement philosophy involving all employees in small, incremental positive changes.
Workplace organization methodology: Sort, Set in order, Shine, Standardize, Sustain.
Visual scheduling system for lean manufacturing and just-in-time production that controls workflow through visual signals.
Error-proofing technique designed to prevent mistakes or make them immediately obvious in manufacturing processes.
Visual signaling system indicating the status of a production line, allowing operators to stop production when problems occur.
Methodology for reducing setup and changeover time to under 10 minutes in manufacturing operations.
Lean management tool visualizing all steps in a manufacturing process to identify waste and optimize flow.
Systematic approach to investigating deviations, identifying root causes, implementing corrections, and preventing recurrence.
Any departure from approved procedures, instructions, specifications, or established standards during manufacturing.
A result that falls outside established acceptance criteria or specifications, requiring investigation.
A result showing a statistically significant trend away from historical data, though still within specification limits.
Systematic process of identifying the fundamental reason for a deviation or problem to prevent recurrence.
Iterative interrogative technique to explore cause-and-effect relationships by repeatedly asking 'why' to identify root cause.
Top-down deductive failure analysis method using Boolean logic to identify pathways leading to system failure.
Formal system to evaluate, approve, and document changes to processes, equipment, materials, or systems.
Integrative framework linking product stability data, regulatory compliance requirements, and change management decisions.
Process of transferring knowledge, methods, and documentation from development to manufacturing or between manufacturing sites.
Process of increasing batch size from development scale to commercial manufacturing scale while maintaining product quality.
Document detailing the step-by-step manufacturing instructions for producing a specific batch of product.
Document detailing the packaging instructions and operations for a specific batch of finished product.
The approved template or reference document from which individual batch manufacturing records are generated.
Digital version of batch manufacturing and packaging records compliant with 21 CFR Part 11 requirements.
An electronic sound, symbol, or process attached to a record that has the same legal significance as a handwritten signature.
The degree to which data are complete, consistent, accurate, trustworthy, and reliable throughout the data lifecycle.
Data integrity principles: Attributable, Legible, Contemporaneous, Original, Accurate, plus Complete, Consistent, Enduring, Available.
Chronological record providing documentary evidence of the sequence of activities that created, modified, or deleted a record.
Any combination of text, graphics, data, audio, pictorial, or other information represented in digital form that is created, modified, or maintained.
Detailed written instructions describing how to perform an activity or process consistently to achieve uniform quality.
Detailed step-by-step instructions for performing a specific task, derived from an SOP.
The approved composition and instructions for manufacturing a pharmaceutical product, including quantities and process parameters.
The document listing all materials and their quantities required to manufacture a specific batch size.
Complete list of raw materials, components, and quantities required to manufacture a pharmaceutical product.
Documented requirements for materials, processes, equipment, or products including acceptance criteria and test methods.
Official document providing test results and specifications compliance for a specific batch of material or product.
Document certifying that a product or material conforms to specified requirements and standards.
Any substance used in the manufacturing of a pharmaceutical product before it undergoes any processing.
Material produced during manufacturing steps between the raw material and finished product stages.
The completed pharmaceutical product before final packaging into commercial containers.
The final pharmaceutical product packaged in its intended container with labeling, ready for distribution.
Status of materials or products held pending quality review and decision, physically segregated from approved stock.
Official decision to approve a batch of product for distribution after confirming compliance with specifications.
Official decision to reject a batch that fails to meet specifications or quality requirements.
Temporary cessation of production or batch movement pending investigation or decision.
Reprocessing of a batch through one or more steps of the manufacturing process to correct a deviation.
Reprocessing of a previously manufactured batch by repeating a step or procedure not originally included in the approved process.
Action to retrieve distributed product that may be defective or non-compliant with regulatory requirements.
Written, electronic, or oral communication alleging deficiencies related to the identity, quality, purity, or potency of a product.
Any untoward medical occurrence associated with the use of a pharmaceutical product, regardless of causal relationship.
Activities relating to the detection, assessment, understanding, and prevention of adverse drug reactions.
Controlled environment equipment for conducting stability studies at specified temperature and humidity conditions.
Standardized temperature and humidity conditions defined by ICH for pharmaceutical stability testing (Zone I-IV).
Hot and humid climate zone (30°C/75% RH) for long-term stability testing, applicable to regions like India.
Subtropical climate zone (25°C/60% RH) for long-term stability testing, applicable to most of Europe and North America.
Stressful storage conditions (40°C±2°C/75%±5% RH) used to predict stability behavior over longer periods.
Standard storage conditions for stability testing representing the intended storage environment for the product.
Storage conditions (30°C/65% RH) used for long-term testing in Zone IV or when justified by deviation from long-term conditions.
The period during which a pharmaceutical product remains within its approved specifications when stored under defined conditions.
The date after which the product should not be used, based on stability data and shelf life determination.
The date after which raw materials or intermediates should be retested for compliance before use.
The quantity of product produced in a single manufacturing run as defined in the batch formula.
A distinctive combination of numbers and/or letters assigned to identify and trace a specific quantity of material or product.
A unique identifier assigned to a specific batch for traceability throughout manufacturing, testing, and distribution.
The date on which the manufacturing of a batch is completed.
The date on which the final packaging operation for a batch is completed.
Inventory management method where oldest stock is used or distributed first to minimize expiry-related waste.
Inventory management method where materials or products closest to expiry are used or distributed first.
Determination of the percentage of theoretical output actually achieved during manufacturing.
The maximum amount of product that can be produced from a given quantity of raw materials under ideal conditions.
The quantity of product actually produced from a given quantity of raw materials.
The ratio of actual yield to theoretical yield, expressed as a percentage.
Procedure to ensure all materials, components, and documents from the previous batch are removed before starting a new batch.
Documented evidence that equipment is suitable for its intended use through installation, operational, and performance qualification.
Documented evidence that a computerized system consistently performs according to its intended use and specifications.
Umbrella term for Good Practice quality guidelines and regulations including GMP, GLP, GCP, GDP, and GVP.
The submission of regulatory dossiers to health authorities for product approval or variation changes.
The complete package of documents submitted to regulatory authorities for marketing authorization approval.
FDA application for approval of a generic drug, demonstrating bioequivalence to the reference listed drug.
FDA application for approval to market a new pharmaceutical product, including full safety and efficacy data.
Confidential document submitted to FDA containing detailed information about manufacturing processes, facilities, or materials.
Standardized format for regulatory submissions defined by ICH for drug registration applications.
Electronic version of CTD submissions using XML backbone for regulatory filing to health authorities.
